**Reasoning summary:**

The 5×5 grid has area 25, partitioned into 5 rectangles with integer side lengths (each side ≤ 5), all with distinct dimension-pairs (rotation identified). I need to maximize the product of the 5 areas.

**Key observation:** List all dimension pairs (a,b), 1≤a≤b≤5, with their areas:
- 1: (1,1); 2: (1,2); 3: (1,3); 4: (1,4),(2,2); 5: (1,5); 6: (2,3); 8: (2,4); 9: (3,3); 10: (2,5); 12: (3,4); 15: (3,5); 16: (4,4); 20: (4,5); 25: (5,5).

Only **area 4** has two distinct dimension-pairs: (1,4) and (2,2). Every other area has exactly one. So in any valid partition, at most one area value repeats, and if it does, it must be 4 (appearing exactly twice).

**Case A — all 5 areas distinct, sum 25:** The product is maximized by values clustered near 5. The most balanced distinct 5-tuple summing to 25 is {3,4,5,6,7} (product 2520), but 7 is not an available area. The best feasible tuple is {2,4,5,6,8}, product = 1920 < 2304.

**Case B — area 4 appears twice:** areas {4,4,a,b,c} with a+b+c = 17, a,b,c distinct, none equal to 4. Maximize 16·abc. Checking all distinct triples from {1,2,3,5,6,8,9,10,12,15,...} summing to 17:
- {1,6,10}→60; {2,3,12}→72; {2,5,10}→100; {2,6,9}→108; {3,5,9}→135; **{3,6,8}→144**.
Max is 144, giving 16·144 = **2304**.

**Construction achieving 2304** (areas 8, 4, 3, 6, 4; dimensions 2×4, 1×4, 1×3, 2×3, 2×2):

- 2×4: rows 1–2, cols 1–4 (area 8)
- 1×4: row 3, cols 1–4 (area 4)
- 1×3: col 5, rows 1–3 (area 3)
- 2×3: rows 4–5, cols 1–3 (area 6)
- 2×2: rows 4–5, cols 4–5 (area 4)

Verification: every cell of the 5×5 grid is covered exactly once; all five dimension-pairs {(2,4),(1,4),(1,3),(2,3),(2,2)} are distinct; areas sum to 8+4+3+6+4 = 25; product = 8·4·3·6·4 = 2304.

---

## Proof

We partition a $5\times 5$ grid (area $25$) into $5$ rectangles whose sides lie on the unit gridlines, with all five dimension-pairs distinct (a rectangle $a\times b$ is identified with $b\times a$). We maximize the product of the five areas.

**Available rectangles.** Every rectangle has integer side lengths $a,b$ with $1\le a\le b\le 5$. The complete list of dimension-pairs and areas is:
$$\begin{array}{c|c}
(a,b) & \text{area}\\ \hline
(1,1)&1,\ (1,2)&2,\ (1,3)&3,\ (1,4)&4,\ (2,2)&4,\\
(1,5)&5,\ (2,3)&6,\ (2,4)&8,\ (3,3)&9,\ (2,5)&10,\\
(3,4)&12,\ (3,5)&15,\ (4,4)&16,\ (4,5)&20,\ (5,5)&25.
\end{array}$$

**Lemma (uniqueness of the repeated area).** Among all areas achievable by a rectangle with sides in $\{1,\dots,5\}$, only area $4$ admits two distinct dimension-pairs, namely $(1,4)$ and $(2,2)$. Every other area has a unique dimension-pair. Consequently, in any valid partition, at most one area value is repeated, and if it is repeated, that value is $4$, occurring exactly twice (using both $(1,4)$ and $(2,2)$).

*Proof of lemma.* Direct inspection of the table above: area $4$ appears twice, all other areas appear once. $\square$

By the lemma, every valid partition falls into one of two cases.

**Case A: all five areas are distinct.** We choose $5$ distinct values from $\{1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12,15,16,20,25\}$ summing to $25$, maximizing their product. By the balancing principle (product maximized when terms are as equal as possible), the optimal distinct real $5$-tuple summing to $25$ is $\{3,4,5,6,7\}$ (product $2520$), but $7$ is not an available area. The most balanced feasible tuple is $\{2,4,5,6,8\}$, with product
$$2\cdot 4\cdot 5\cdot 6\cdot 8 = 1920.$$
Any other feasible distinct $5$-tuple summing to $25$ (e.g. $\{2,3,5,6,9\}\to 1620$, $\{2,3,4,6,10\}\to 1440$, $\{1,4,5,6,9\}\to 1080$) has a strictly smaller product. Hence Case A yields at most $1920$.

**Case B: area $4$ is repeated.** The five areas are $\{4,4,a,b,c\}$ with $a,b,c$ distinct, none equal to $4$, and $a+b+c = 25-8 = 17$. We maximize $16\cdot abc$. Enumerating all distinct triples from the available set (excluding $4$) that sum to $17$:
$$\{1,6,10\}\!(60),\ \{2,3,12\}\!(72),\ \{2,5,10\}\!(100),\ \{2,6,9\}\!(108),\ \{3,5,9\}\!(135),\ \{3,6,8\}\!(144).$$
The maximum is $abc = 144$ from $\{3,6,8\}$, giving
$$16 \times 144 = 2304.$$
The corresponding rectangles are $(2,2),(1,4),(1,3),(2,3),(2,4)$ — five distinct dimension-pairs, as required.

Since Case A gives at most $1920 < 2304$, the global maximum (if Case B is realizable) is $2304$.

**Realizability.** We exhibit a tiling of the $5\times 5$ grid achieving $2304$. Index rows $1$–$5$ (top to bottom) and columns $1$–$5$ (left to right). Place:
- a $2\times 4$ rectangle in rows $1$–$2$, columns $1$–$4$ (area $8$);
- a $1\times 4$ rectangle in row $3$, columns $1$–$4$ (area $4$);
- a $1\times 3$ rectangle in column $5$, rows $1$–$3$ (area $3$);
- a $2\times 3$ rectangle in rows $4$–$5$, columns $1$–$3$ (area $6$);
- a $2\times 2$ rectangle in rows $4$–$5$, columns $4$–$5$ (area $4$).

Every unit cell is covered exactly once (rows $1$–$2$: columns $1$–$4$ by the $2\times4$ and column $5$ by the $1\times3$; row $3$: columns $1$–$4$ by the $1\times4$ and column $5$ by the $1\times3$; rows $4$–$5$: columns $1$–$3$ by the $2\times3$ and columns $4$–$5$ by the $2\times2$). The five dimension-pairs $\{(2,4),(1,4),(1,3),(2,3),(2,2)\}$ are pairwise distinct, the areas sum to $8+4+3+6+4=25$, and the product is
$$8\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 6\cdot 4 = 2304.$$

**Conclusion.** The maximum possible economic score is $\boxed{2304}$.

## Proof

We partition a $5\times 5$ grid (area $25$) into $5$ rectangles whose sides lie on the unit gridlines, with all five dimension-pairs distinct (a rectangle $a\times b$ is identified with $b\times a$). We maximize the product of the five areas.

**Available rectangles.** Every rectangle has integer side lengths $a,b$ with $1\le a\le b\le 5$. The complete list of dimension-pairs and areas is:
$$\begin{array}{c|c}
(a,b) & \text{area}\\ \hline
(1,1)&1,\ (1,2)&2,\ (1,3)&3,\ (1,4)&4,\ (2,2)&4,\\
(1,5)&5,\ (2,3)&6,\ (2,4)&8,\ (3,3)&9,\ (2,5)&10,\\
(3,4)&12,\ (3,5)&15,\ (4,4)&16,\ (4,5)&20,\ (5,5)&25.
\end{array}$$

**Lemma (uniqueness of the repeated area).** Among all areas achievable by a rectangle with sides in $\{1,\dots,5\}$, only area $4$ admits two distinct dimension-pairs, namely $(1,4)$ and $(2,2)$. Every other area has a unique dimension-pair. Consequently, in any valid partition, at most one area value is repeated, and if it is repeated, that value is $4$, occurring exactly twice (using both $(1,4)$ and $(2,2)$).

*Proof of lemma.* Direct inspection of the table above: area $4$ appears twice, all other areas appear once. $\square$

By the lemma, every valid partition falls into one of two cases.

**Case A: all five areas are distinct.** We choose $5$ distinct values from $\{1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12,15,16,20,25\}$ summing to $25$, maximizing their product. By the balancing principle (product maximized when terms are as equal as possible), the optimal distinct real $5$-tuple summing to $25$ is $\{3,4,5,6,7\}$ (product $2520$), but $7$ is not an available area. The most balanced feasible tuple is $\{2,4,5,6,8\}$, with product
$$2\cdot 4\cdot 5\cdot 6\cdot 8 = 1920.$$
Any other feasible distinct $5$-tuple summing to $25$ (e.g. $\{2,3,5,6,9\}\to 1620$, $\{2,3,4,6,10\}\to 1440$, $\{1,4,5,6,9\}\to 1080$) has a strictly smaller product. Hence Case A yields at most $1920$.

**Case B: area $4$ is repeated.** The five areas are $\{4,4,a,b,c\}$ with $a,b,c$ distinct, none equal to $4$, and $a+b+c = 25-8 = 17$. We maximize $16\cdot abc$. Enumerating all distinct triples from the available set (excluding $4$) that sum to $17$:
$$\{1,6,10\}\!(60),\ \{2,3,12\}\!(72),\ \{2,5,10\}\!(100),\ \{2,6,9\}\!(108),\ \{3,5,9\}\!(135),\ \{3,6,8\}\!(144).$$
The maximum is $abc = 144$ from $\{3,6,8\}$, giving
$$16 \times 144 = 2304.$$
The corresponding rectangles are $(2,2),(1,4),(1,3),(2,3),(2,4)$ — five distinct dimension-pairs, as required.

Since Case A gives at most $1920 < 2304$, the global maximum (if Case B is realizable) is $2304$.

**Realizability.** We exhibit a tiling of the $5\times 5$ grid achieving $2304$. Index rows $1$–$5$ (top to bottom) and columns $1$–$5$ (left to right). Place:
- a $2\times 4$ rectangle in rows $1$–$2$, columns $1$–$4$ (area $8$);
- a $1\times 4$ rectangle in row $3$, columns $1$–$4$ (area $4$);
- a $1\times 3$ rectangle in column $5$, rows $1$–$3$ (area $3$);
- a $2\times 3$ rectangle in rows $4$–$5$, columns $1$–$3$ (area $6$);
- a $2\times 2$ rectangle in rows $4$–$5$, columns $4$–$5$ (area $4$).

Every unit cell is covered exactly once (rows $1$–$2$: columns $1$–$4$ by the $2\times4$ and column $5$ by the $1\times3$; row $3$: columns $1$–$4$ by the $1\times4$ and column $5$ by the $1\times3$; rows $4$–$5$: columns $1$–$3$ by the $2\times3$ and columns $4$–$5$ by the $2\times2$). The five dimension-pairs $\{(2,4),(1,4),(1,3),(2,3),(2,2)\}$ are pairwise distinct, the areas sum to $8+4+3+6+4=25$, and the product is
$$8\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 6\cdot 4 = 2304.$$

**Conclusion.** The maximum possible economic score is $\boxed{2304}$.
